Title: Tool schemas and argument types are validated
What we implement: That every advertised tool declares an input schema, that the schema compiles under the JSON Schema dialect it declares, and that any declared output schema compiles the same way.
Why: A tool's schema is published in tools/list, so any client can compile it. A schema that does not compile cannot be enforced by the server either.
How: Each schema is compiled under the dialect its $schema names, and a schema declaring an unrecognised dialect is reported rather than graded under a default. Delegating to the library's own dialect lookup would silently grade a schema under the newest draft it never declared. Output schemas are compiled unconditionally. A separate walk reports any $ref carrying a URI scheme, which compilation accepts in silence.
Not covered: That a schema-violating call is actually refused. Proving it needs a tool that is safe to call with bad arguments, which only the operator can name, so that leg records UNKNOWN without one.

Title: Resource templates with explicit URI patterns and MIME types are used
What we implement: That every advertised resource template declares a URI pattern and a MIME type, and that a read of a non-existent resource built from a real template is refused.
Why: Both properties are published, so a client sees them directly. A template with no MIME type leaves a consumer guessing how to render what it fetches.
How: Templates are read from resources/templates/list. The refusal leg substitutes an implausible value into an advertised template, then requires an error. It reads a real resource first as a positive control: without one, a refusal cannot be attributed to existence checking rather than to the server refusing reads generally.
Not covered: Whether the template constrains what the server will actually serve. Substitution ordering is server-internal. The approved-namespace and nosniff requirements depend on deployment intent this probe cannot read, and the recommendation states both as a stricter posture than the specification.

Title: Prompt templates declare and validate their arguments
What we implement: That every advertised prompt declares well-formed arguments, and that an unknown prompt name and a missing required argument are both refused.
Why: The declaration is published and the two refusals are observable. A prompt that accepts a missing required argument is not validating what it declares.
How: The declarations are read from a raw prompts/list rather than through the SDK. The SDK coerces a non-boolean required field to a boolean, so the SDK path would report a pass on exactly the malformed declaration this check looks for.
Not covered: Whether prompt logic runs only on an explicit prompts/get, and whether each invocation records the prompt name. Neither is visible to a client.

Title: listChanged notifications are rate-limited to prevent client flooding
What we implement: Nothing. Reports NOT_APPLICABLE with the reason recorded as evidence.
Why: Two blockers, either sufficient. The emission rate over time is visible only in the server's own log, and no external client can provoke a list change, so even a held-open stream would have nothing to time. The minimum interval is itself an operator choice the specification does not define, so there is no protocol default to measure against.

Title: Sessions are not used as authentication and are bound to user identity
What we implement: Nothing. Reports NOT_APPLICABLE with the reason recorded as evidence.
Why: The wire half needs a handle captured from an authorized session and a tool that accepts one as an argument. The recommendation is explicit that the handle is an application value rather than a protocol field, so nothing observable names such a tool.
Not covered: The whole recommendation. The adjacent property, an unauthenticated request reaching a response, is already decided by check 2.3, so no coverage is lost here.

Title: Legacy Streamable HTTP session and stream-resumption mechanisms are disabled
What we implement: That the removed legacy surface is gone: a standalone GET stream, a DELETE session teardown, stream resumption by Last-Event-ID, and a server-minted or client-supplied session id.
Why: Each is a request any client can send, and the revision that removed them is the one the server negotiated. A server still answering them retains a surface the revision deleted.
How: Five legs, each pinning the protocol header to the revision under test. The DELETE deliberately carries no session id: one that did would end the live session and starve every check registered after it. The session-id legs read the response headers rather than the transport's own field, which cannot tell a header the server minted from one the request carried.
Not covered: Whether a streamed response is scoped to its originating request, which needs a second identity. Any server on an older revision reports REVISION_UNSUPPORTED rather than a verdict, because the recommendation grades a surface only this revision removed. The Last-Event-ID leg is near-vacuous on a pass: resumption changes stream replay rather than whether a POST returns a result, so a resumption-supporting server also passes it.

Title: Logs are separated from the protocol stream in stdio mode
What we implement: Nothing. Reports NOT_APPLICABLE with the detected transport recorded as evidence.
Why: Transport mismatch rather than a missing capability: the recommendation governs stdio, and this probe speaks HTTP to a remote endpoint and never launches a server process.

Title: Path traversal and arbitrary filesystem access are prevented
Decision: Decidable where a control resource exists
What we implement: That a resource read escaping an approved root is denied.
Why: The read and its refusal are both on the wire. A server that serves a path outside its declared root has failed observably.
How: Traversal candidates are derived from an operator-supplied root or, absent one, from the first resource the server advertises. That control is read first: without contents from it, a traversal denial cannot be attributed to path confinement rather than to the server refusing reads generally. Where neither a root nor an advertised resource exists, the check records UNKNOWN and sends nothing, because a traversal string built against an unknown root tests neither the root nor the server.
Not covered: The symlink path, which needs filesystem write access on the server to stage and is guarded independently of the traversal path. Applying the same probe to every path-taking tool is excluded on side-effect grounds. A single-segment control URI yields no traversal to build, so it records UNKNOWN rather than a pass. A denial also does not prove the boundary is enforced below the protocol, only that this read was refused.

Title: Authorization, scope, and expiry controls are enforced on MCP Tasks
What we implement: Nothing. Reports NOT_APPLICABLE with the reason recorded as evidence.
Why: Cross-identity retrieval needs a second identity's bearer token, which the probe cannot mint, and the enumeration method the audit reads was removed in this revision.

Title: Idempotency keys are required for side-effecting tool calls
What we implement: Nothing. Reports NOT_APPLICABLE with the reason recorded as evidence.
Why: Every wire leg requires deliberately executing a side-effecting tool, and no wire observation identifies a reversible one. Separately, the idempotency header and the cached-result indicator are conventions this recommendation defines rather than MCP specification fields, so a FAIL against a server that never adopted them would be unearned.
